analysis.one_liner: Caps small-loan interest at 36% APR and bans holding car titles or bank-account access as loan collateral.
analysis.headline: A House bill to cap short-term loan rates at 36% APR drew only 4 cosponsors and died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap interest at a 36% annual percentage rate on short-term consumer loans of $3,000 or less — the market where payday and car-title lenders charge rates that often reach several hundred percent a year. It would also bar lenders from taking a borrower's bank-account access or car title as collateral, ban "remotely created checks" that pull money from an account without a signature, void any contract that breaks these rules, and leave states free to keep stricter laws. The bill never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who take out small, short-term loans. A 36% APR cap would replace fees that can equal 400% a year or more on two-week payday loans. Banning account-access and car-title security would stop lenders from automatically debiting borrowers' bank accounts or repossessing vehicles when a loan comes due. Banning remotely created checks would close a way to pull money from an account without the account holder's signature. Contracts made in violation would be unenforceable, and states could keep or add tougher rules [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps the interest rate on covered loans of up to $3,000 — short-term loans with terms of about 91 days or less — at a 36% annual percentage rate, with all fees counted toward that rate so lenders cannot disguise the true cost.
Makes it unlawful to secure these loans with access to a borrower's deposit account or with a vehicle title, removing the two main levers payday and title lenders use to force repayment.
Bans remotely created checks — checks drawn on a customer's account without that customer's signature — a payment tool associated with unauthorized withdrawals.
Declares contracts made in violation of the act unenforceable against consumers, and explicitly preserves any stronger state consumer-protection laws rather than overriding them.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, car-title lenders, and banks offering deposit-advance style products, which would lose the fee revenue that comes from rates far above 36% APR. Some subprime borrowers would also bear a cost in a different form: if lenders stop offering short-term loans they cannot profit from at 36%, those borrowers lose a legal source of emergency cash [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: A 36% annual cap is a very thin margin on a two-week loan — pennies per dollar lent — so lenders say they simply could not offer these small short-term loans profitably. The practical risk is that borrowers with poor credit lose their legal emergency-credit option and fall back on bounced-check fees, unlicensed lenders, or going without.

The bill carves out pawnbroker loans: a non-recourse pawn loan secured by goods handed over to the pawnbroker stays outside the cap, so pawn shops could keep charging effective rates above 36% on the same small-dollar borrowers the bill targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the benefits are direct and large: a 36% ceiling plus a ban on holding bank-account access and car titles would end the debt-trap structure of the payday and title-loan business. The honest cost is access: some high-risk borrowers who today use payday loans would have nowhere legal to go, and the pawnbroker carve-out leaves one high-cost channel open. The design is fairly standard for state-level rate caps, several of which already operate at or below 36%. The bill's real weakness was political, not substantive — it never got a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never came up again before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Gabrielle Giffords introduced the Predatory Lending Sunset Act on July 1, 2010, with Rep. Jared Polis as an original cosponsor; four Democratic members cosponsored in total.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction and received no further action — no markup, no hearing listed, no floor vote.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday and auto-title lenders came out ahead: without a federal rate cap, they kept charging triple-digit annual rates on small loans. The borrowers the bill aimed to protect gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Gabrielle Giffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap small-loan rates at 36% APR and ban title and account-access lending.

for.name: Rep. Jared Polis
for.what_they_did: Joined Giffords in introducing the bill on its first day.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Barney Frank, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote; it sat in committee from July 2010 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Payday and auto-title lending industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal 36% rate caps on small-dollar lending, which would eliminate the fee model the industry is built on.

sides.party_line_note: All five House supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows whether any Republicans would have backed it.

industries.note: Their core product — two-week loans secured by a check or bank debit, typically costing 400% APR or more — would be unlawful under the 36% cap and the ban on account-access collateral. The bill's entire purpose was to shut this business model down.

The bill bars taking a vehicle title as security, ending the practice of repossessing borrowers' cars over small loans. Borrowers would keep their transportation; lenders would lose their collateral leverage.

industries.industry: Retail banks offering deposit-advance and check products
industries.note: The bill bans securing small loans with account access and outlaws remotely created checks, closing bank channels into the same short-term high-fee lending. Banks lose a fee stream, though they have other business lines to fall back on.

The bill explicitly exempts non-recourse pawn loans secured by goods the customer hands over, so pawn shops keep making high-cost small loans outside the 36% cap while their payday-style competitors are shut down — a carve-out that locks in their position in the small-dollar credit market.
